title: The Neo-Assyrian Empire
subtitle: 911–609 BC · The First World Empire — the Recovery, the Sargonid Century, the Library of Nineveh, and the Twenty-Year Collapse

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The recovery from the dark age, the terror-campaigns of Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III, the refounding of the state by Tiglath-Pileser III, the Sargonid dynasty and its capitals, and the twenty-year collapse

entries.label: The recovery — Ashur-dan II to Adad-nirari II
entries.hint: Beginning with Ashur-dan II, a run of kings clawed the kingdom back from the dark age — retaking the Jazira from the Aramaean statelets, resettling the abandoned land, rebuilding the towns, and restoring the yearly campaign as the rhythm of the state. Their inscriptions frame it as a return: bringing 'the exhausted people of Assyria' home and pushing the border back out to where the fathers had held it.
entries.note: A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian Rulers of the Early First Millennium BC I' (RIMA 2, 1991); Karen Radner, 'Ancient Assyria: A Very Short Introduction' (2015).

entries.label: Ashurnasirpal II — the terror and the showpiece
entries.hint: Ashurnasirpal II drove west to the Mediterranean with a cruelty his own annals dwell on — flayed rebels, pillars of severed heads, cities burned. He then moved the capital to Kalhu and built the Northwest Palace, its state rooms lined with carved stone reliefs, and marked its opening with a ten-day banquet for 69,574 people, itemised on a stone stele. Calculated terror abroad and calculated magnificence at home became the Assyrian method.
entries.note: Grayson, RIMA 2 (1991); the Banquet Stele and the Northwest Palace from the Nimrud excavations (Layard; Mallowan).

entries.label: Shalmaneser III — the long reach and the first check
entries.hint: Shalmaneser III campaigned for thirty-four years. At Qarqar in 853 he met a coalition of a dozen Levantine kings — Damascus, Hamath, Ahab of Israel — and, though his annals claim victory, he did not break through the west for years. His Black Obelisk shows Jehu of Israel prostrate with tribute. He brought Babylon under Assyrian protection. His last years brought a great revolt and the start of the 'age of the magnates'.
entries.note: Grayson, RIMA 3 (1996); the Kurkh Monolith and the Black Obelisk (British Museum).

entries.label: The age of the magnates
entries.hint: For eighty years the kings were weak and the empire was run by its great provincial governors — men like the commander-in-chief Shamshi-ilu, who campaigned and set up monuments in his own name. Plague, a total solar eclipse taken as an omen of catastrophe, and repeated revolt marked the period. Assyria shrank back toward its heartland, and the crown's authority nearly dissolved.
entries.note: J. A. Brinkman on the period; the Saba'a and Tell al-Rimah stelae; the Assyrian eponym chronicle for 763 (the Bur-Sagale eclipse).

entries.label: The queens — Sammu-ramat and Naqia
entries.hint: Assyrian royal women could hold real power. Sammu-ramat, mother of Adad-nirari III, appears on a boundary stele beside her son and campaigned with the army — she is the historical seed of the Greek legend of Semiramis. A century later Naqia, wife of Sennacherib and mother of Esarhaddon, engineered her son's and then her grandson's succession and imposed a loyalty oath on the empire in her own name.
entries.note: The Pazarcık stele (Sammu-ramat); Sarah Melville, 'The Role of Naqia/Zakutu in Sargonid Politics' (1999); the 'Zakutu Treaty' (SAA 2, no. 8).

entries.label: Tiglath-Pileser III — the refounder
entries.hint: Tiglath-Pileser III took the throne in a coup and rebuilt the state from the ground up: he broke the over-mighty provinces into small districts under directly appointed governors, many of them eunuchs; he made the army a permanent professional force; he systematised two-way mass deportation; he annexed conquered kingdoms as provinces instead of leaving native vassals; and he took the throne of Babylon himself. He is the true founder of the imperial system.
entries.note: Hayim Tadmor & Shigeo Yamada, 'The Royal Inscriptions of Tiglath-pileser III' (RINAP 1, 2011); Radner (2015).

entries.label: Sargon II — the usurper who named himself for Akkad
entries.hint: Sargon II seized the throne in the disorder after Shalmaneser V and adopted a throne-name recalling Sargon of Akkad. He destroyed the Kingdom of Israel and deported its people, crushed the rival kingdom of Urartu, fought Merodach-Baladan for Babylon, and built an entirely new capital from bare ground, Dur-Sharrukin. Then he was killed in battle in Anatolia and his body was never recovered — a disaster his son read as divine punishment.
entries.note: Grant Frame, 'The Royal Inscriptions of Sargon II' (RINAP 2, 2021); the 'Letter to the God Ashur' on the eighth campaign against Urartu.

entries.label: Sennacherib — Nineveh and the razing of Babylon
entries.hint: Sennacherib abandoned his father's ill-omened new city and made Nineveh the greatest capital in the world — the 'Palace Without Rival', an 80-kilometre canal system, and a terraced garden that some identify with the 'Hanging Gardens'. He besieged Hezekiah's Jerusalem in 701 and pulled back without taking it. And in 689 he did the unthinkable: he razed Babylon, flooded the site, and carried its gods away. His own sons murdered him.
entries.note: A. K. Grayson & Jamie Novotny, 'The Royal Inscriptions of Sennacherib' (RINAP 3, 2012–14); John Malcolm Russell, 'Sennacherib's Palace Without Rival at Nineveh' (1991).

entries.label: Esarhaddon — the rebuilder and the conqueror of Egypt
entries.hint: Esarhaddon won a civil war against his brothers, then reversed his father's great crime by rebuilding Babylon — a theological about-face carefully justified in his inscriptions. In 671 he invaded Egypt, took Memphis, and drove out the Kushite pharaoh Taharqa, briefly making Assyria a two-continent empire. Sick, anxious and hemmed in by omens, he bound the whole empire by oath to accept his sons as heirs — the Succession Treaty.
entries.note: Erle Leichty, 'The Royal Inscriptions of Esarhaddon' (RINAP 4, 2011); Simo Parpola & Kazuko Watanabe, 'Neo-Assyrian Treaties and Loyalty Oaths' (SAA 2, 1988).

entries.label: Ashurbanipal — the scholar-king at the peak
entries.hint: Under Ashurbanipal the empire reached its greatest extent. He sacked Thebes in 663; he crushed and finally destroyed Elam, sacking Susa in 646; he fought a four-year war against his own brother, the king of Babylon, that ended with the brother dead in the burning palace. He also built at Nineveh the first systematic library, a project to gather every kind of written knowledge — and he boasted, uniquely for a king, that he could read it.
entries.note: Jamie Novotny & Joshua Jeffers, 'The Royal Inscriptions of Ashurbanipal' (RINAP 5, 2018–); the library in Frame & George, 'The Royal Libraries of Nineveh' (2005).

entries.label: The twenty-year collapse
entries.hint: After Ashurbanipal's death the empire fell apart with astonishing speed. His sons Ashur-etil-ilani and Sin-shar-ishkun fought over the throne; Babylon broke free under Nabopolassar in 626; the Medes under Cyaxares allied with him. Ashur fell in 614, Nineveh was sacked in 612, and a last Assyrian king, Ashur-uballit II, made a doomed stand at Harran with Egyptian help. By 609 the largest empire the world had known simply no longer existed.
entries.note: The 'Fall of Nineveh Chronicle' (ABC 3); the prophet Nahum; the speed of the collapse discussed in Eckart Frahm (ed.), 'A Companion to Assyria' (2017).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The reconquest of the west and Qarqar, the long war with Urartu, the fall of Israel and the siege of Jerusalem, the destruction of Babylon, the conquest of Egypt and Elam, and the brothers' war and the fall of Nineveh

entries.label: The reconquest of the west and Qarqar
entries.hint: Ashurnasirpal II reached the Mediterranean and washed his weapons in the sea; Shalmaneser III tried to break through the Levantine kingdoms and, at Qarqar on the Orontes in 853, fought the largest coalition Assyria had yet faced — Damascus, Hamath, Israel and nine others, fielding thousands of chariots. Assyria claimed the field but could not hold the west for another decade, when Damascus finally submitted and Jehu of Israel paid tribute.
entries.note: Grayson, RIMA 2–3; the Kurkh Monolith account of Qarqar; the Black Obelisk.

entries.label: The long war with Urartu
entries.loc: Lake Van and the Armenian highlands
entries.hint: Urartu, a mountain kingdom around Lake Van, was Assyria's most serious rival for a century and a half — a fortress state that contested the northern frontier and the horse and metal trade of the highlands. Sargon II's eighth campaign in 714, described at length in a 'letter to the god Ashur', shattered Urartu's army and sacked the temple-city of Musasir. Urartu survived but never threatened Assyria again.
entries.note: The 'Letter to the God Ashur' (Frame, RINAP 2, 2021); Paul Zimansky, 'Ecology and Empire: The Structure of the Urartian State' (1985).

entries.label: The fall of Damascus and Israel
entries.hint: Tiglath-Pileser III annexed the northern Levant, took Damascus in 732, and turned the coastal and hill kingdoms into provinces. His successors finished the work: after a three-year siege the capital of the Kingdom of Israel, Samaria, fell in 722–720, and Sargon II deported its people east and settled others in their place. The 'ten tribes' of Israel disappear from history here, and Judah is left alone as an Assyrian vassal.
entries.note: RINAP 1 (Tadmor & Yamada 2011); RINAP 2 (Frame 2021); the Israelite side in 2 Kings 15–17.

entries.label: Sennacherib and the siege of Jerusalem
entries.hint: In 701 Sennacherib crushed a revolt of the western vassals, stormed the Judahite fortress of Lachish — a siege carved slab by slab across a whole room of his palace — and shut up King Hezekiah in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage'. Then he withdrew without taking the city. The Assyrian annals record heavy tribute and pass over the retreat in silence; the Hebrew Bible attributes the deliverance to a plague sent by the angel of the Lord.
entries.note: RINAP 3 (Grayson & Novotny 2012); the Lachish reliefs (British Museum); the Judahite account in 2 Kings 18–19 and Isaiah 36–37.

entries.label: The destruction of Babylon
entries.hint: After years of Babylonian revolt and the loss of a son to Elamite captivity, Sennacherib took Babylon and did what no Mesopotamian king had done to the holy city: he tore it down, dug canals to flood the site, ploughed salt into the ground, and carried the statue of Marduk away. It was regarded across Mesopotamia as monstrous sacrilege, and Assyrian tradition itself later read Sennacherib's murder as the gods' revenge for it.
entries.note: RINAP 3; the Bavian inscription; the 'Marduk Ordeal' text and the theological reaction analysed by Eckart Frahm.

entries.label: Egypt and the end of Elam
entries.hint: Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal ruled Egypt for two decades, sacking Thebes in 663 and carrying off its wealth — an event the Hebrew prophet Nahum recalls. Ashurbanipal then broke Elam in a series of campaigns, sacked Susa in 646, desecrated its royal tombs, and carried the statue of the goddess Nanaya home after 1,635 years. A famous relief shows him feasting in a garden with the severed head of the Elamite king hanging in a tree.
entries.note: RINAP 5; the sack of Thebes in Nahum 3:8–10; the Elamite war reliefs from the North Palace (British Museum).

entries.label: The brothers' war and the fall of Nineveh
entries.hint: The empire's downfall began with a civil war: Ashurbanipal's brother Shamash-shum-ukin, king of Babylon, rebelled in 652 and was besieged into starvation, dying in the flames in 648. A generation later Nabopolassar's Babylon and Cyaxares' Medes joined forces. Ashur fell in 614; in 612 the allied army stormed Nineveh after a three-month siege and burned it. The last stand at Harran in 610 was the empire's final act.
entries.note: The 'Fall of Nineveh Chronicle' (ABC 3); the war with Shamash-shum-ukin in the Ashurbanipal inscriptions (RINAP 5).
